newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: INTERVIEW-PROFESSOR SVEJNAR ON CZECH CROWN OUTLOOK.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-PROFESSOR SVEJNAR ON CZECH CROWN OUTLOOK.

text.p: Below are excerpts of a Reuters interview conducted on Thursday with Jan Svejnar, director of the Economics Institute of the Czech Academy of Sciences and professor of economics at the University of Michigan:

SVEJNAR: "I think that it is not so important for the central bank to devalue the currency actively. What I am more worried about is that with the trade deficit and current account deficit reaching eight percent of GDP now, the situation will sooner or later become untenable in the sense that the western capital investors who have caused a significant inflow of capital here -- which is what's keeping the country in balance -- and they will start pulling their resources out. When that happens there will be a natural depreciation of the crown.
"I think the problem will start when it reaches the bottom limit... What I am concerned about is that it is crucial that the central bank not intervene and give up its foreign currency reserves."

"To make even a stronger point, I think that it should probably not intervene too much if it starts hitting the bottom limit. It is essentially the British situation (in 1992). When George Soros intervened against the British pound, the British Government and the British Central Bank, with the assistence of other central banks intervened. Essentially, (the Bank of England) lost a signficant part of its reserves and they had to devalue the pound or let the pound devalue anyway.

"I think that the Czechs should take a lesson from this and be ready let the crown depreciate if such forces are there rather than give up the labouriously established foreign exchange reserves which are very good and very useful, and they should keep them."
(REUTERS: Are you troubled by the current state of Czech foreign reserves being at about five months of import cover?)

"They have to keep them, imagine if you lost them overnight because your trying to intervene, then you're going to have to let the currency depreciate anyway because you no longer have reserves, and you have no cushion to work with in case there is some external shocks."

"The Czechs adopted a fixed exchange rate as a strategy. It was a daring move and it worked so far and they accumulated these reserves. Another very successful or very advanced tranforming economy, the Slovene economy, they started with no reserves, and that's why they adopted a crawling peg. They had to accumulate reserves and they did not want to lose them by central bank operations."
(REUTERS: In the Czech situation, would a crawling peg similar be advisable?)

"That would be one of the options. But I don't think that it would have to be (used) yet in the sense that we have some leeway in which the exchange rate can move (within the central bank's flotation band), but I think that if the currency starts really some major gyrations, and if the peg is no longer a valid yardstick, then I think all options, including a crawling peg should be considered."
(REUTERS: Do you think, given the track record of the Czech central bank that if the crown does depreciate through a steady outflow that they will intervene?)

"I think that they are debating this right now and my advice is that they should not intervene, and keep their reserves because they are just too small compared to the forces out there in the specualtive investor field. The British central bank together with the western European central banks were too small when it came to that fateful night. So I don't think (the Czech central bank) has the resources to intervene in a major way."
(REUTERS: If the crown breaks through a depreciation of 7.5 percent below parity, how much lower could it go before it gets dangerous and they have to intervene?)

"I don't think they have to intervene at all. I think there is a very strong equilibrating mechanism. I wouldn't be surprised if it went down to a 20 percent differential for instance. It is quite natural. If you look at how the real exchange rate has appreciated over the last several years... it certainly reaches double digits in terms of differential (against the mark/dollar basket).

"The problems that Czech exports have been having in the world together with the major wave of imports that have been coming here basically testifies to the world of real goods and capital flows which are very volatile and could go either way."
(REUTERS: Just to be clear, you are not suggesting a direct devaluation taken by the government or central bank but rather letting the market depreciate the currency naturally?)
"I'm not saying that the central bank should go and devalue. I'm saying that it should be ready to let the currency depreciate if and when the investors move the rate."
(REUTERS: With the slowing in output we saw in January... where should the impetus come from to solve these problems?)

"We have a very heterogenous situation. Some firms are restructuring and are doing very well other haven't restructred as much and have major problems. I think the crux of the issue... is that while the government, by and large, has eliminated the subsidies it used to give to firms, the banking sector has not yet developed to the point where it can assess projects properly and establish tight lending policies. So some firms are getting money for projects that are not viable and where faster intervention would be more desirable.

"I also see a major problem in the application of legal norms and the development of a legal system in the financial field. What I have in mind is bankruptcy procedings. We see very little bankruptcy. We have problems in terms of corporate governance where we need much stronger pressure on managers to restructure from the owners, and better procedures for the control of managers.

"All these together have translated into a kind of lethargic performance at a time when it's really crucial for the Czech economy to be growing rapidly. If you do simple calculations for this country to start approaching the European Union (levels) within a quarter century or so, you really need seven or eight percent real growth, and it's feasible. This economy has the potential."

(REUTERS: But the debate is now raging between growth versus inflation -- the central bank opting for tight monetary policy whereas the prime minister, Mr. Klaus, is pushing the need for growth more and more. Where do you stand on this?)

"I've always stressed over the last several years that growth is the important thing. The trade off, whether you reduce inflation by two percentage points or whether you increase growth by two percentage points -- I would go for the faster rate of growth at this point. We have a hard time measuring inflation in the United State, let alone here.
"I think healthy growth based on the restructuring of producers and the reallocation of resources -- that I think is the priority for the next decade."
(REUTERS: Would you recommend a rate cut or an easing of minimum reserve requirements?)

"I would not go for tighter monetary policy. As the experience indicated last summer with the tightening up, some of the smaller financial instutions do get crowded out... that edges out small and medium sized producers.
"I think it's advisable that the central bank hold the steady course, not tighten more, and go for stimulating growth.
"I would at this point keep the course, and then start thinking if rates could be reduced gradually. I would say a timeframe of about a year -- within a year to start reducing."
-- John Mastrini, Prague Newsroom, 420-2-2423-0003
